text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. Could you please describe the lesion you are concerned about, including its appearance, size, and how long it has been present? Also, have you noticed any changes in its color, shape, or borders recently?

speaker: Patient
text: 62-year-old male. The patient has recently immigrated to the US from Africa and seeks evaluation for a non-healing, red, crusty lesion on the shaft of his penis and a similar lesion on his left middle finger. Previous treatments in his home country for syphilis and eczema have been unsuccessful. The patient is a smoker, with a history of two packs per day for the last 30 years.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given the non-healing nature of these lesions and your smoking history, I need to assess for potential malignancy. Have you experienced any pain, bleeding, or discharge from either the penile or finger lesion, and have you noticed any swelling in the lymph nodes of your groin or armpit?

speaker: Doctor
text: The biopsy findings of nuclear hyperchromasia, multinucleation, and increased mitotic figures are highly suggestive of a viral-induced malignancy or pre-malignant condition, likely related to HPV. To confirm the specific viral etiology and guide treatment, I need to identify the viral subtype. REQUEST TEST: HPV DNA testing (specifically for high-risk types 16 and 18) on biopsy specimens.

speaker: Doctor
text: The negative HPV test and biopsy findings of koilocytosis (multinucleation) with atypia in a patient from an endemic region strongly suggest Erythroplasia of Queyrat, a form of squamous cell carcinoma in situ, rather than a benign viral wart. text: Past medical history: No known malignancies or hereditary diseases in the family. Previous treatments for syphilis and eczema. Social history: Lives with his 4th wife, smokes 2 packs of cigarettes per day for the last 30 years, has recently immigrated from Africa.

speaker: Doctor
text: The clinical presentation of velvety red plaques on the penis and finger, combined with biopsy evidence of atypia and a negative HPV test, points towards Squamous Cell Carcinoma in situ (Erythroplasia of Queyrat on the penis).
